::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## The decision this serves
Two decisions, both consequential. *Is this number comparable to that number?* —
across studies, species, assays and papers. And *should this drug be dosed per
kilogram or flat?* — which determines every dose in every protocol that follows.
:::

## 1. Why this lesson exists

Unit errors are the most common serious mistake in this field, and the most
embarrassing, because they are invisible: the model converges, the plots look
fine, the report reads well, and the number is wrong by a factor of a thousand.

They survive review because reviewers check the *modeling* and assume the
*arithmetic*. Nobody re-derives your ng/mL. So the defence has to be structural,
not vigilance:

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Three rules that prevent almost all of it.**

1. **Units live in the variable name or the column metadata, never in your
   head.** `conc_ng_ml`, not `conc`. `CL_L_h`, not `CL`.
2. **Do dimensional analysis on every equation before you trust it.** If the
   left side is L/h, the right side must be too. This takes ten seconds and
   catches most structural mistakes as well as unit ones.
3. **Convert once, at the boundary.** Convert on the way into the analysis
   dataset and never again. Mixed units inside an analysis are how a factor of
   1000 gets in.
:::

## 2. Amounts, concentrations, and one convenient coincidence

Differential equations track **amounts**; observations are **concentrations**.
Keeping the two straight in your head is the single most useful habit in
`S0-01`'s notebook.

There is a coincidence worth exploiting deliberately:

$$\frac{\mu\text{g}}{\text{L}} = \frac{\text{ng}}{\text{mL}}$$

So if you express doses in micrograms and volumes in litres, the compartment
amount divided by the volume comes out directly in ng/mL — the unit almost every
bioanalytical laboratory reports for a small molecule. Every simulation in these
lessons does this, and it is why `50 mg` appears in the code as `50 * 1000`.

For a large molecule the natural unit is usually mg/L (= µg/mL), so express
doses in mg and keep volumes in L. Pick the convention per compound, write it in
the header of the script, and do not mix.

## 3. Mass versus molar

Mass concentration is what the assay reports. Molar concentration is what
pharmacology means — receptor occupancy, K~i~, K~d~, IC~50~ and every *in vitro*
number you will want to compare against are molar.

$$C\,[\text{nM}] = \frac{C\,[\text{ng/mL}]}{MW\,[\text{g/mol}]} \times 1000$$

For Ozanib ($MW = 465$ g/mol), a steady-state trough of 51.9 ng/mL is 112 nM and
a peak of 560.7 ng/mL is 1206 nM. If the *in vitro* IC~50~ is 200 nM, you now
know something real: the trough sits below it and the peak well above, so this
is a compound whose coverage question is about time above threshold, not about
peak. **That inference is unavailable until you convert.**

Two traps:

- **Biologics.** A monoclonal antibody has MW ≈ 150,000 g/mol, so 10 µg/mL is
  only ~67 nM. Mass concentrations that sound enormous are molar concentrations
  that are not. Target-mediated disposition arithmetic (`S1`) is molar and
  cannot be done in mass units.
- **Salt factor.** A dose stated as the salt is not the dose of the free base.
  A 100 mg salt dose of a compound with a salt factor of 1.18 delivers 84.7 mg
  of active moiety. Get this wrong and every clearance estimate is off by 18%.
  It is written in the investigator's brochure, not in the dataset.

## 4. Free versus total

Assays usually report **total** drug; only unbound drug is pharmacologically
active and only unbound drug is what a mechanistic model should compare against
an *in vitro* potency.

$$C_u = f_u \times C_{total}$$

Ozanib's $f_u$ is 0.08, so a 1206 nM total peak is a 96 nM free peak — below a
200 nM IC~50~ rather than six-fold above it. Same data, opposite conclusion.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Free concentration, not free fraction.** These are routinely conflated, and
Smith, Di & Kerns argue the confusion actively misdirects drug discovery
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/nrd3287)): *in vivo* efficacy is governed by the
unbound concentration at the target, whereas compounds are frequently
prioritised on unbound *fraction* measured *in vitro*. Optimising $f_u$ does not
itself raise the free concentration, so selection on that basis can advance the
wrong candidate.

For a modeller the operational rule is narrow: report and compare **unbound
concentrations**; treat $f_u$ as a conversion factor, never as a potency
surrogate.

The free drug hypothesis is also not universal. Deviations are documented in
hepatic uptake, where observed unbound intrinsic clearance exceeds prediction —
the plasma protein-mediated uptake effect, reviewed by Schulz, Stresser & Kalvass
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1080/03602532.2023.2195133)). Several of the candidate
mechanisms for that effect remain consistent with the free drug hypothesis, so
the review sharpens it rather than discarding it. `P-08` returns to this.
:::

### $f_u$ is a variable that is usually treated as a constant

The conversion above uses a single number, 0.08, as though it were a property of
the molecule. Two literatures say otherwise, and both matter more than their
obscurity suggests.

**It varies with concentration, and not always in the obvious direction.**
Saturable binding raising $f_u$ as concentration rises is textbook. Nation,
Theuretzbacher and Tsuji catalogue drugs that do the opposite — $f_u$ *falls* as
concentration rises ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejps.2018.07.004)). Either
way, a single $f_u$ applied across a dose range that spans saturation is an
assumption, not an arithmetic step, and it should be stated as one.

**It varies between patients, systematically.** Serum albumin is low in
40–50% of critically ill patients, and for highly bound antibacterials the
consequences are not subtle: reviewing the clinical literature, Ulldemolins and
colleagues report that ceftriaxone's apparent volume of distribution and
clearance were both increased roughly two-fold in hypoalbuminaemic critically ill
patients ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.2165/11539220-000000000-00000)), with
ertapenem failing its pharmacodynamic target as a result. The mechanism is the
one this section just described, running in a population rather than a
spreadsheet.

The operational consequence for `CASE-SM` is small but real: the free
concentrations derived here inherit whatever uncertainty sits in $f_u$, and the
model report should say where the value came from and over what range it was
measured.
Whenever you compare a clinical concentration to an *in vitro* potency, state
explicitly which of the four combinations you are using (total or free,
clinical or *in vitro*); the mismatch is a standard reviewer question and a
standard source of over-optimistic translational claims.

## 5. Units of clearance, and the per-kilogram question

Clearance is a volume per time. Three conventions coexist and all three appear
in the literature:

| Convention | Ozanib | Where you see it |
|---|---|---|
| L/h | 12 L/h | Population PK reports, labels |
| mL/min | 200 mL/min | Physiology, renal and hepatic comparisons |
| L/h/kg | 0.171 L/h/kg | Preclinical work, interspecies scaling |

Comparing a clearance to physiology is one of the most useful sanity checks
available: hepatic blood flow is roughly 90 L/h (1500 mL/min) and glomerular
filtration around 7.5 L/h (125 mL/min). An apparent oral clearance of 12 L/h is
comfortably below hepatic blood flow, so nothing is obviously impossible. An
estimate of 200 L/h would mean either extra-hepatic elimination or — far more
likely — an error. Note the word *apparent*: with $CL/F$ you can only conclude
that $CL \le CL/F$, since $F \le 1$.

## 6. Allometry — what it is, and what it is not

Larger animals clear drugs faster in absolute terms and slower per kilogram.
The empirical regularity is a power law in body weight:

$$P_i = P_{ref} \left(\frac{W_i}{W_{ref}}\right)^{\theta}$$

with $\theta \approx 0.75$ for flow-like parameters ($CL$, $Q$) and
$\theta \approx 1$ for volumes ($V_c$, $V_p$). `CASE-SM` is generated with
exactly these values, so you can check your own recovery of them.

**Where it works.** As a prior structure for a covariate model in adults; as a
first-pass interspecies projection for first-in-human dose; as the standard,
expected parameterisation that a reviewer will look for.

**Where it fails — and these matter.**

- **Young children.** Below roughly two years, organ *maturation* dominates
  size. Clearance per kilogram rises through infancy and then falls; a pure
  size model will badly under-dose neonates. The standard fix is a maturation
  function on top of allometry.
- **Obesity.** Total body weight over-predicts clearance for many drugs because
  adipose tissue is not metabolically equivalent. Lean or fat-free mass often
  performs better, and which descriptor wins is an empirical question, not a
  theoretical one.
- **Narrow weight ranges.** This is the one that catches everyone, and the
  notebook demonstrates it on real generated data. Fitting $\theta$ freely in a
  typical adult population — where weight spans maybe 50 to 120 kg — gives an
  estimate with wide uncertainty. In `CASE-SM`, a regression on the *true*
  individual clearances of the 46 subjects without a CYP3A4 inhibitor recovers
  $\theta = 0.93$ against a truth of 0.75. Not because the model is wrong, but
  because 30% between-subject variability over a two-fold weight range does not
  contain enough information.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
This is why most population PK analyses **fix** the allometric exponents at
0.75 and 1 rather than estimating them, and it is a defensible choice you should
be able to justify out loud: the exponents are supported by broad external
evidence, and the data in a single adult study cannot improve on that.
:::

### Confounding, demonstrated

Run the same regression on all 60 subjects, ignoring that a quarter of them are
on a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, and the estimated exponent inflates to 1.15. The
inhibitor lowers clearance; in this dataset the inhibitor-treated subjects also
happen to sit slightly differently on the weight axis, and weight absorbs the
effect. **A covariate you omit does not disappear — it redistributes itself into
the covariates you kept.** This is the central hazard of covariate modeling and
you will meet it properly in `S2`.

### Where the physiological numbers come from

Allometric and maturation models need reference values — organ weights, blood
flows, tissue composition, plasma protein concentrations, enzyme abundance — and
those numbers have to come from somewhere. For adults the standard sets are
long-established. For a preterm neonate they are not, and Abduljalil and
colleagues assembled them precisely because they existed in no single source:
organ sizes expressed as functions of body weight so that variability and
correlation are retained, protein binding as a function of age, and ontogeny
functions for CYP1A2, CYP3A4 and CYP2C9
([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40262-019-00825-6)).

Two things are worth taking from it beyond the numbers themselves. The paper is
explicit that **tissue composition values are thin**, which is the kind of
statement a parameter source rarely volunteers and a modeller should always look
for. And it shows what a system-parameter dataset is: a separate, citable object
from the drug model built on top of it. When `S3` asks where a PBPK model's
physiology came from, this is the shape of the answer.

## 7. Per-kilogram or flat dosing?

An old argument with a quantitative answer: weight-based dosing is worth the
operational cost only if body weight explains enough of the variability in
exposure to matter.

For `CASE-SM`, using the true individual clearances, AUC across the population
has a CV of **51.5%** under flat 50 mg dosing and **44.1%** under weight-based
0.7 mg/kg dosing. The 95th-to-5th percentile spread narrows from 4.3-fold to
3.5-fold. Real, but modest — because body weight explains only part of the
variability and the rest is unexplained between-subject variation that no dosing
rule can touch.

Whether that improvement justifies per-kilogram dosing depends on the
therapeutic index, not on the CV. For a wide-index compound, flat dosing wins on
every practical ground: fewer dosing errors, simpler packaging, no weighing, no
compounding. For a narrow-index compound the same 7 percentage points may be
decisive. **The analysis tells you the size of the effect; the therapeutic
window tells you whether it matters.** Confusing those two is a common error in
early clinical development.

## Work through it

- [Notebook — R](notebook-r.qmd)
- [Notebook — Python](notebook-py.qmd)

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```r
MW <- 465                                   # g/mol
ng_ml_to_nM <- function(x, mw) x / mw * 1000

conc <- c(trough = 51.9, peak = 560.7)      # ng/mL
ng_ml_to_nM(conc, MW)                       # -> 111.6, 1205.8 nM
ng_ml_to_nM(conc * 0.08, MW)                # free, fu = 0.08
```

### Python

```python
MW = 465.0                                  # g/mol

def ng_ml_to_nM(x, mw):
    return x / mw * 1000

conc = {"trough": 51.9, "peak": 560.7}      # ng/mL
{k: ng_ml_to_nM(v, MW) for k, v in conc.items()}      # -> 111.6, 1205.8 nM
{k: ng_ml_to_nM(v * 0.08, MW) for k, v in conc.items()}  # free, fu = 0.08
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Failure mode — the assay that changed units mid-study
A long study switches bioanalytical laboratories at month 14. The new laboratory
reports in µg/L; the old one reported in ng/mL. These are numerically identical,
so nothing breaks — this time.

Now imagine the new laboratory reports µg/mL. The last third of the dataset is
1000-fold lower than the first two thirds. Every diagnostic will look strange,
the residual error will inflate, and a modeler under deadline pressure will
reach for a time-varying clearance term or a second error model and *find one
that fits*. The model will be wrong and defensible-looking.

The defence is not vigilance. It is a **units column carried through the
assembly pipeline**, and a data check that fails loudly when more than one unit
appears for one analyte. `S0-03` builds exactly that check.
:::

## Check yourself

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. A paper reports an mAb trough of 10 µg/mL and an in vitro K~d~ of 2 nM. Is the target saturated?
Convert first. At MW ≈ 150,000 g/mol, 10 µg/mL = 10 mg/L ÷ 150,000 g/mol ≈
67 nM total — about 33-fold above a 2 nM K~d~ on a total basis. But the
comparison should be made on free drug, and for a target-mediated compound a
large fraction may be bound to target at low concentrations. The honest answer:
probably yes at this trough, and the right way to confirm it is a
target-mediated disposition model with target occupancy as an output, not a
ratio of two numbers.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Your PopPK gives $CL/F$ = 250 L/h. What do you check before believing it?
250 L/h is nearly three times hepatic blood flow, so as a *true* clearance it
would require substantial extra-hepatic elimination. With `/F` it is not
impossible — low bioavailability inflates apparent clearance, and $F = 0.05$
would make true clearance 12.5 L/h. So: check the units of the dose column,
check for a salt-factor correction, check whether dose was recorded in mg while
concentration was in µg/mL, and only then consider low bioavailability. In
practice the unit error is far more common than the biology.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. You estimate an allometric exponent of 1.15 in adults. What are the three explanations, in order of likelihood?
(a) There is not enough information in the weight range to estimate it — the
confidence interval almost certainly includes 0.75; (b) an omitted covariate
correlated with weight is loading onto the weight term, which is exactly what
happens in `CASE-SM` when the CYP3A4 inhibitor is ignored; (c) the true
relationship really is steeper than 0.75, which does occur but is the last
explanation to reach for, not the first. Fix the exponent at 0.75, model the
missing covariate, and see whether anything remains.
:::

- **Next:** [S0-03 · Data assembly](../s0-03-data-assembly/) — where the units
  actually get fixed.
- **Uses this:** `S1` (molar arithmetic for TMDD), `S3` (allometry and
  maturation in pediatric PBPK), `S2` (covariate modeling and confounding).
- **Reference:** Anderson BJ, Holford NHG, *Mechanistic basis of using body size
  and maturation to predict clearance in humans*
  ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.2133/dmpk.24.25)) — the argument for the 0.75 exponent
  and for maturation functions. Then Rhodin MM et al., *Human renal function
  maturation* ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00467-008-0997-5)), which fits GFR
  from premature neonate to adult and shows exactly where size alone fails.
  Rowland & Tozer for the physiological reference values.

*Not just our experience:* the standard TMDD tutorial names this explicitly,
listing "the appropriate conversion between amounts and concentrations for drugs
and system species and associated rate constants" among the practical issues
that "can easily lead to erroneous results" (Dua, Hawkins & van der Graaf,
[DOI](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.41)). When a peer-reviewed tutorial stops to
warn about unit conversion, it is not a beginner's problem.

*Seen in the wild:* a first-in-human dose was once calculated from a preclinical
clearance reported in mL/min/kg and read as L/h/kg. The error was caught at a
protocol review by someone who compared the projected clearance to hepatic blood
flow and said "that can't be right." That comparison takes five seconds and
should be reflexive.
